subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Knowing When to Think More
description: One-minute skill: Knowing When to Think More.

hook.text: A chess grandmaster uses intuition for 95% of moves. The remaining 5% get deep calculation.

buildup.text: Expertise means knowing when shortcuts are enough and when to engage slow, effortful analysis.

discovery.text: The skill isn't avoiding heuristics. It's metacognition: knowing which tool fits the current problem.

twist.text: Thinking more about every decision is exhausting and often counterproductive. Deliberation has diminishing returns.

climax.text: Use heuristics for routine choices. Reserve deep thinking for irreversible, high-stakes, unfamiliar decisions.

punchline.text: Think hard about what deserves hard thinking.

quiz.question: When should you override heuristics with deep thinking?

details.summary: Knowing when to think more is the meta-cognitive skill of recognizing when quick heuristic judgment is sufficient versus when a problem demands slow, deliberate analysis. The best decision-makers are not those who always think carefully but those who know when careful thinking pays off.
details.whyItMatters: Both over-thinking and under-thinking are costly. Over-thinking wastes time, creates analysis paralysis, and does not improve accuracy in simple situations. Under-thinking in complex or high-stakes situations leads to avoidable errors.
takeaways: Not every decision warrants deep analysis and not every decision can rely on intuition
High stakes, novel situations, and low time pressure all favor deliberate thinking
Familiar, low-stakes, time-pressured situations favor heuristic shortcuts

faq.question: How do you know when a heuristic shortcut is good enough?
faq.answer: When the decision is low-stakes, reversible, time-pressured, and involves a familiar domain, heuristics work well. When stakes are high, the decision is irreversible, time is available, and the domain is unfamiliar, invest in deliberate analysis.

faq.question: Can expertise change when to rely on intuition?
faq.answer: Yes. Experts in familiar domains have earned their intuitions through thousands of feedback cycles. A chess grandmaster's gut feeling is reliable because it draws on vast experience. A novice's gut feeling in the same domain is not similarly reliable.
